title: Money already spent
principle: Ignore money already spent. Count what you could do instead.

screens.text: Let me start with an airline. In 1932, JRD Tata flew a small plane carrying mail from Karachi to Bombay. That was the start of the airline that became Air India. Decades later, the government owned it, and by 2021 it was losing money every day.

screens.prompt: In 2021, how much do you think Air India was costing the government each day?
screens.why: About ₹20 crore a day. That's what the government official in charge of the sale said in October 2021, when he explained why the sale had to finish quickly.

screens.title: Selling after so much
screens.text: Since 2009, the government had put ₹54,584 crore of cash into Air India. In October 2021, it agreed to sell the airline back to the Tata group. Tata paid ₹2,700 crore in cash and took on ₹15,300 crore of Air India's debts.

screens.title: The sunk cost trap
screens.text: Some people said: after putting in so much, selling now wastes it. But that money was already gone, whatever happened next. A sunk cost is money already spent that you cannot get back. Spending more because you already spent a lot is the sunk cost fallacy, a common mistake.

screens.prompt: Someone says, "The government put ₹54,584 crore into Air India. Selling it now wastes all that money." What's wrong with this?

options.label: Nothing. Selling turns the money into a real loss
Air India could still earn it all back

screens.why: Right. Keeping Air India would not bring back the ₹54,584 crore. It would only add about ₹20 crore of new losses every day. The choice was about the future, not the past.

wrong.a: It feels that way, but the money was lost before the sale, not because of it. Selling only stopped more losses.
wrong.c: It had lost money for years. Keeping it meant about ₹20 crore of new losses a day, with no sign of the old money coming back.

screens.title: Now look at your business
screens.text: Air India had planes and crores of rupees, but a small shop can make the same mistake. Imagine you run a juice stall. Last year, you paid ₹40,000 for a big juicer. It is slow, it breaks often, and you lose fruit every time it does.

screens.prompt: Your brother says, "We paid ₹40,000 for the old juicer. Use it until it dies." What should decide your choice?

options.label: What a new one costs and saves from now on
Whether the old one still runs

screens.why: Yes. Using the old juicer longer won't bring back the ₹40,000. What you can still change is what you spend and save from now on.

wrong.a: That's the sunk cost fallacy. The ₹40,000 is gone whether you keep the old juicer or not. Only what you spend and save from now on can change.
wrong.c: It still runs, but it costs you in repairs and wasted fruit every month. Compare that with what a new one costs and saves.

screens.prompt: A new juicer costs ₹15,000. The old one sells for ₹8,000. The new one saves ₹2,000 a month. How many months to earn it back?
screens.why: Well done. You spend ₹15,000 and get ₹8,000 back, so changing juicers costs ₹7,000. At ₹2,000 a month, that's 3½ months. The ₹40,000 you paid last year isn't in the sum at all.

wrong.b: Close. But you also get ₹8,000 for the old juicer. So the switch costs ₹15,000 − ₹8,000 = ₹7,000, and ₹7,000 ÷ ₹2,000 is 3½ months.
wrong.c: That's ₹40,000 ÷ ₹2,000, but the ₹40,000 is already spent. The switch costs ₹15,000 − ₹8,000 = ₹7,000, which pays back in 3½ months.

screens.prompt: I'll show you six things about the old juicer. For each one, tell me: should it change your choice today?

items.text: The ₹8,000 it would sell for today
₹2,000 a month lost to repairs and fruit
₹2,000 you spent fixing it last month
The ₹15,000 price of a new one
The week you spent choosing it last year

screens.why: That's it. What already happened can't change: the price you paid, old repairs, and time spent choosing. Only what you can still get, spend or save should decide.

screens.title: What else could you do?
screens.text: There's a second idea. Your stall sells to people walking by, but the gyms nearby buy 50 bottles at a time. Every hour at the counter is an hour you can't spend getting gym orders. The best thing you give up is called the opportunity cost.

screens.prompt: Afternoon counter sales leave you ₹200. Your cousin will run the counter for ₹150. Visiting gyms then would earn ₹400. Who should stand there?

options.label: Nobody. Close the counter in the afternoons
My cousin. My time is worth more at the gyms

screens.why: Exactly. With your cousin there, you keep ₹200 − ₹150 = ₹50 from the counter, plus ₹400 from the gyms: ₹450. Standing there yourself gives only ₹200. The ₹400 you give up is the opportunity cost.

wrong.a: That gets you ₹200. Your cousin costs ₹150, but frees you to earn ₹400 at the gyms, so you end up with ₹450.
wrong.b: That gets you ₹400 from the gyms. Keeping the counter open with your cousin adds ₹50 more, so ₹450 in all.

screens.setup: You opened a second stall in a mall and spent ₹1.2 lakh on its counter, fridges and signs. You spend your afternoons there. Three months later, it still loses ₹10,000 a month. A smoothie chain offers ₹30,000 for your counter and fridges, if you decide this week.
screens.question: What do you do with the mall stall?

options.label: Keep going, or the ₹1.2 lakh is wasted
options.outcome: You keep the stall open for six more months and lose ₹60,000 more. Then you close it anyway, and the smoothie chain has taken another space.
options.why: The ₹1.2 lakh was gone either way. Keeping the stall open only added ₹10,000 of new losses every month.
options.better: Take the ₹30,000 this week, close the stall, and put your afternoons into the gym orders.

options.label: Take the ₹30,000 and close it
options.outcome: You get ₹30,000 back and stop the ₹10,000 monthly loss. You spend your free afternoons winning gym orders for your first stall.
options.why: Well done. You judged the choice by what comes next, not by what you had already spent. And you moved your time to where it earns more.

options.label: Cut its hours and wait six months
options.outcome: Shorter hours cut the loss to ₹6,000 a month. After six months, you've lost ₹36,000 more, the crowd still hasn't grown, and the smoothie chain has taken another space.
options.why: Cutting the loss was sensible. But the crowd had already had three months to grow, and waiting cost you ₹36,000 plus the ₹30,000 offer.
options.better: Take the ₹30,000 this week, while the offer stands.

screens.text: Money you've already spent is a ___ cost. Decide by what comes ___, not by what's gone.
screens.why: Exactly. The money in Air India, your old juicer and your mall stall were all spent already. Only what comes next can still change, so that's what should decide.

summary: Sunk cost fallacy: spending more because you already spent a lot.
Money already spent is gone either way. Decide by what comes next.
Opportunity cost is the best thing you give up. Your time matters too.

cards.front: You paid ₹50,000 for a machine you no longer need. Someone offers ₹20,000. What should decide whether you sell?
options: The ₹20,000 offer, and what keeping it costs
cards.back: The ₹50,000 is a sunk cost. Only what you can still get or save counts.

cards.front: A ₹12,000 upgrade saves ₹3,000 a month. How long to earn it back?
A helper costs ₹200. In that time you could win orders worth ₹600 of profit. What does doing the work yourself really cost?
cards.back: ₹600, the profit you give up. That's the opportunity cost.
